source.title: 'Mogging' is Collins' word of the year... but do you know what it means?
source.summary: The slang term, which relates to outshining or upstaging someone, is one of 10 words celebrated.
source.evidence_text:
"Mogging", a word used playfully to mean outshining, outperforming or upstaging someone or something, has been named as word of the year by the Collins English Dictionary.
Mogging - not to be confused with mugging or mugging someone off - refers to outshining or dominating someone, most often in looks.
A fast-growing slang word among members of Generations Z and Alpha - both online and in everyday conversation - mogging went mainstream in 2026 with a 210% increase in its usage.
But it now has a much more mainstream usage, as a playful put-down or a compliment, depending on the context.
Collins - one of the UK's major dictionary publishers - draws from a range of sources, including social media, to reflect how the English language is evolving in the UK each year.
Collins' managing director Alex Beecroft said its lexicographers look at "how often words are used" and also "analyse patterns of usage" that reveal the latest linguistic trends.
The selection of mogging as word of the year, he said, "shows how each generation leaves its mark on language".
Other definitions that made the dictionary's 10-strong shortlist included ghost job, something frustrated jobseekers will be familiar with - when an employer posts a position with no intention of appointing someone.
Its word of the year for 2025 was "vibe coding" - the art of making an app or website by describing it to artificial intelligence (AI) rather than by writing programming code manually.
The word is often traced back to the acronym AMOG, standing for Alpha Male of the Group, and has been variously associated with bodybuilding forums in the mid-2010s as well as the manosphere and incels.
It can be seen and heard in looks maxxing communities -online groups where people swap advice on how to maximise their physical attractiveness.

grammar.explanation: Use “has” or “have” + “been” + a past participle to describe a completed action with a result that matters now. The subject receives the action. In “has been named”, the focus is on the word receiving the title; “by” introduces who made the decision.

grammar.concept: Emphatic qualification with “far from” and an -ing form
grammar.explanation: Use “far from” followed by an “-ing” form to emphatically reject a description. Here, “far from being invariably insulting” rejects the idea that the term is always insulting, while allowing both insulting and complimentary uses.
grammar.example_quote: Far from being invariably insulting, the term can function as either a playful put-down or a compliment, depending on context.

quiz.question: Which statement best captures the central development reported in the brief?
options: Collins has recognised a rapidly spreading slang term whose interpretation varies with context.
Collins has established a single complimentary meaning for a previously insulting expression.
Collins has concluded that informal language is replacing other forms of English.
option_feedback: The recognition follows wider circulation, while the reading preserves the distinction between insulting and complimentary uses.
The term can function as either an insult or a compliment; the recognition does not establish one exclusive meaning.
The reading describes the spread of one expression, without claiming that informal language is replacing other forms.

quiz.question: What does the reported 210% increase establish?
options: That 210% more dictionary entries were devoted to the term.
That the term’s recorded use increased substantially.
That every generation adopted the term at the same rate.
option_feedback: The percentage concerns how much the term was used, rather than the number of dictionary entries.
The statistic supports substantial growth in use, although the reading provides no absolute counts.
The reading identifies Generations Z and Alpha as prominent users but gives no comparison of adoption rates across generations.

quiz.question: Which supported reason explains why the lexicographers’ methods involve more than counting appearances of a word?
options: They also examine recurring contexts to identify developments in language.
They also establish whether speakers approve of the dictionary.
They also require expressions to lose their informal meanings.
option_feedback: The reading describes both frequency and recurring contexts as evidence used to identify linguistic developments.
The reading does not describe dictionary approval as part of the method.
Nothing in the reading suggests that an expression must lose its informal meanings to be recognised.

quiz.question: Which account most accurately preserves the reading’s qualification about the term’s history?
options: Its origin in bodybuilding forums has been conclusively established.
Its historical connections are irrelevant to any interpretation of the word.
It is often linked to an earlier acronym and has connections with bodybuilding forums.
option_feedback: The reading reports a connection with bodybuilding forums, which does not conclusively establish an origin there.
The reading supplies historical context without claiming that this context is irrelevant.
This preserves the qualified account of an earlier acronym and the distinction between association and proven origin.

quiz.question: What interpretation does “far from being invariably insulting” support?
options: The term has ceased to carry any insulting meaning.
The term’s insulting meaning is possible but not universal.
The term is complimentary whenever physical appearance is involved.
option_feedback: Rejecting an invariably insulting meaning allows exceptions; it does not eliminate insulting uses.
The sentence explicitly allows both a playful insult and a compliment.
The reading says appearance is a frequent focus, but it does not make appearance a guarantee of complimentary intent.

quiz.question: Which hypothetical example most closely reflects the appearance-related sense described in the reading?
options: Someone attracts more admiration for their appearance than the person beside them.
Someone asks an online group for advice without comparing themselves with anyone.
Someone records how frequently a new expression appears in conversation.
option_feedback: The comparison captures the idea of one person appearing more impressive than another.
Seeking advice may fit the communities described, but it does not itself demonstrate the comparative meaning of the term.
This illustrates language research, rather than the appearance-related sense.

quiz.question: How does the reading present social media’s role in Collins’ work?
options: As the authority that formally chooses the winning expression.
As the exclusive record of how English changes.
As one contribution to a broader body of evidence.
option_feedback: The reading identifies Collins as making the choice and does not assign that authority to social media.
The publisher uses varied material, so social media is not presented as exclusive.
Social media contributes to the varied material used to reflect changes in English.

quiz.question: Which distinction is essential to the reading’s definition of a “ghost job”?
options: The employer takes longer than applicants expect to appoint someone.
The employer advertises without intending to appoint someone.
The employer intends to recruit but receives no suitable applications.
option_feedback: A delay alone does not establish the absence of an intention to appoint someone.
The defining feature is the employer’s intention when advertising the position.
An unsuccessful recruitment attempt still involves an intention to appoint, which differs from the definition given.

quiz.question: What distinguishes “vibe coding” in the reading?
options: Describing an intended app or website to artificial intelligence instead of manually writing its code.
Manually writing code and then describing the finished product to users.
Advertising a programming position without intending to recruit.
option_feedback: The reading defines “vibe coding” through instructions to artificial intelligence in place of manually writing programming code.
This reverses the distinction made in the reading.
This resembles the separate definition of a “ghost job” rather than the development method described.

quiz.question: Which interpretation best preserves the interpersonal emphasis of “upstaging”?
options: Taking part in the same activity as someone else.
Proving that another person deliberately behaved badly.
Drawing attention away from another person by appearing more impressive.
option_feedback: Shared participation does not include the shift in attention expressed by “upstaging”.
“Upstaging” concerns relative attention or admiration, rather than proving misconduct.
This captures how one person’s presence or performance can overshadow another’s.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses “far from” with an -ing form to preserve the reading’s qualified meaning?
options: Far from convey only criticism, mogging can also express admiration.
Far from conveying only criticism, mogging can also express admiration.
Far from conveyed only criticism, mogging can also express admiration.
option_feedback: The base form “convey” does not fit the taught “far from” construction.
“Conveying” supplies the required “-ing” form, while the sentence allows both critical and admiring uses.
The form “conveyed” does not supply the “-ing” form required in this construction.

options: Generations influence language in distinctive, recognisable ways.
Every generation contributes an equal number of expressions.
Younger speakers control the dictionary’s editorial decisions.
option_feedback: “Leave their mark on” expresses distinctive influence, which the reading presents as Beecroft’s interpretation of the choice.
The phrase concerns influence without quantifying or comparing generations’ contributions.
Influencing language does not establish control over the publisher’s decisions.
